note: The canto opens with the Trinity at the work of creation. The "first Power" is God the Father, who looks on the Son, and the Love that both breathe forth is the Holy Spirit: three persons, one God.

quote: where one celestial motion strikes against another
note: The whole sky turns daily from east to west, in line with the celestial equator. The sun and planets also creep the other way along their own tilted track. Dante points to the place where the two circles cross, which the sun reaches at the spring equinox.
The zodiac, the band of sky that the sun and planets travel, tilted about 23 degrees from the equator.

quote: If their pathway were not bent just so
note: The tilt is what gives the earth its seasons, as the sun moves north and south through the year. Without it, or with a different angle, growth and life below would fail. Dante sees the design of a master craftsman in it.
The reader as a pupil at a school bench, or a guest at table. Dante serves the food and leaves the reader to chew it.
Dante's Italian calls him the "scribe" of his subject: he presents himself as one who writes down what he was shown.
The sun, which passes heaven's power down to the earth more than any other body, and measures out days and years.

quote: joined with that sphere I mentioned above
note: The sun was at the crossing point just described, in the sign of Aries: it is spring. The journey takes place around the spring equinox of 1300, the season in which the world was believed to have been created.
Each day the sun circles the earth a little farther north than the day before, so over the weeks its path is a rising spiral. In spring it also rises earlier each morning.

context: She carries him from heaven to heaven in no time at all, and grows brighter at each one.
The souls here stand out against the sun by being brighter than it, light on light. Dante says he cannot make the reader imagine it.

quote: no eye has ever looked beyond the sun
note: The sun is the brightest thing human sight knows, so imagination has nothing to build on beyond it.
The souls of the fourth heaven. Their reward is to see how the Father begets the Son and breathes forth the Spirit, the mystery of the Trinity that their minds worked on in life.
God. The sun we see is his image in the material world: as it gives light to the eyes, he gives light to minds.
Dante's Italian says she was "eclipsed", an astronomer's word chosen for the heaven of the sun. For the only time in the poem he forgets her, and she is glad, because he forgets her for God.
Twelve lights ring Dante and Beatrice like a crown. A second ring of twelve will form around this one in Canto 12.
Diana, goddess of the Moon, daughter of Latona. The image is the halo that appears around the Moon in misty air.
Anyone who will not rise to Heaven to hear the song for himself might as well ask a mute to describe it.

quote: like stars near the fixed poles
note: The stars near the pole of the sky wheel around it in small, steady circles and never set.
The ascent through the heavens. No one who has been allowed to climb it in life comes down without returning after death: a promise that Dante will be saved.

context: The speaker was a friar of his order.

quote: where souls grow fat if they don't stray
note: A hint that the order has wandered from its founder's road. Dante is puzzled by the phrase, and Thomas spends much of Canto 11 explaining it.

context: Thomas studied under him at Paris and Cologne.
He names the twelve lights of the ring in order, starting from himself. He had been dead twenty-six years in 1300 and was not yet declared a saint.

note: A 12th-century teacher at Bologna whose great collection, the Decretum, put the laws of the Church in order and founded the study of canon law. The "two courts" are usually taken as the law of the Church and the law of the state, which his work brought into agreement.

Peter Lombard (died 1160), bishop of Paris. His Sentences, a gathering of the Church Fathers' teachings in four books, was the standard theology textbook of the universities. In its preface he compares his book to the two small coins of the poor widow in the Gospel, who gave all she had (Luke 21).

context: Not named. The world "hungers for news" because people argued over whether he was saved. The love he breathes recalls the Song of Songs, read as the love of God and the soul.

quote: no second soul ever rose to see so much
note: God told Solomon that there had been none like him before, and none would arise after (1 Kings 3). Dante wonders how that can be true beside Adam and Christ. Thomas explains in Canto 13 that it means wisdom as a king.

context: Not named, but known by his subject: the nature and ranks of the angels.

note: Usually identified as Paulus Orosius, a priest from Spain. About 417, at Augustine's request, he wrote a history of the world to show that its disasters were no worse under Christianity than before. Dante drew much of his ancient history from it. Other names have been proposed.

context: He is not one of the lights in this ring. Dante names him only as the man who made use of the small light's book.
Not named. He was buried at Pavia in the church of San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro, "Saint Peter of the golden ceiling". The Middle Ages honored him as a martyr.

note: Isidore, bishop of Seville (died 636). His Etymologies, an encyclopedia of all knowledge arranged by the origins of words, was a standard reference for centuries.
The Venerable Bede (died 735), a monk in the north of England, a scholar of the Bible and of time-reckoning, and author of the Ecclesiastical History of the English People.
Richard of Saint Victor (died 1173), prior of the abbey of Saint Victor in Paris. He wrote on contemplation, the stages by which the mind rises to the sight of God.

context: The twelfth light, which closes the ring beside Thomas. That Thomas should praise the man he opposed in life, and call his teachings truths, has puzzled readers ever since. In Heaven the old quarrels of the schools are over.

note: The Rue du Fouarre in Paris, where the university's philosophy lectures were given. It was named for the straw the students sat on.
Dante's phrase is "invidiosi veri": truths that were resented, or that made him hated.
One of the earliest descriptions in literature of a mechanical clock with wheels and a chime. Such clocks were a new invention in Dante's lifetime.
The Church, which rises before dawn to sing matins, the first prayers of the day, to Christ her bridegroom. The ring of the wise turns and sings like the wheels of the clock that wakes her.
